## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Niḷinikājātaka* (Ja 526) is a narrative in the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon. According to the opening framing narrative, the Buddha recounted this story while residing at Jetavana to address a monk who had been tempted and led astray by his former wife, reminding him that she had similarly caused him to lose his meditative absorptions in a past life [SuttaCentral].
In the story of the past, Indra is alarmed by the intense ascetic heat (*tapas*) generated by the ascetic Isisiṅga (Isisinga) and withholds rain for three years [Olson 2015]. Blaming the drought on the ascetic's spiritual practice, Indra instructs a king to send his royal daughter, Princess Niḷinikā, to seduce him [Olson 2015]. The princess succeeds in breaking the ascetic's chastity and destroying his mystic meditation [SuttaCentral; Olson 2015].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral identify a full Sanskrit parallel in the Mahāvastu (*The Jātaka of Princess Nalinī*, Mvu 79), as well as an intra-canonical passage-level parallel in the *Campeyyajātaka* (Ja 506) [SuttaCentral]. In automated text-reuse analysis, DharmaNexus records 45 shared passages with the commentary in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Pañcamo bhāgo), comprising nearly 10,000 characters [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also detects algorithmic cross-language alignments with Buddhist texts in Tibetan translation, including the *Lalitavistara* (D0095), the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka* (D0056), and Āryaśūra's *Jātakamālā* (D4150), alongside low-scoring segment matches in the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99) [DharmaNexus].
